messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Ethan, a 38-year-old high school teacher, had always prided himself on his ability to create a safe and welcoming classroom environment. However, after a traumatic mugging three months ago, his world had become a place of constant anxiety and fear. The incident had occurred one evening while he was walking home from his favorite coffee shop. A group of men had approached him, demanding his wallet. He could still taste the bitterness of the coffee he had just sipped, a sensory detail that would return unbidden whenever memories of that night surfaced, flooding his mind with the visceral reality of his terror. Those moments replayed relentlessly, forcing their way into his thoughts at the most inconvenient times, making it impossible for him to focus on anything else.

Since the mugging, Ethan had developed a keen sensitivity to crowded places. He avoided the bustling hallways at school and steered clear of busy shopping malls, acutely aware of how overwhelming the throngs of people could be. The anxiety would grip him, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, a habit that had taken hold the moment he stepped out of his house that night. The vivid memories of the mugging made him feel as if danger lurked behind every unfamiliar face. Each time he was reminded of that night, whether through a crowded hallway or an unexpected sound, the sensation of threat intensified, reinforcing his belief that he was never truly safe. He had come to believe that he could trust no one, a notion that was reinforced each time he felt the weight of a stranger's gaze upon him; he would scrutinize their expressions, searching for any hint of threat. This constant vigilance transformed the world into a perilous place, one where he could no longer feel safe even in familiar surroundings.

Ethan’s struggles with loud noises had also intensified. The sudden sounds would trigger his memories of the chaos during the mugging, making him acutely aware of how vulnerable he felt, and reinforcing his conviction that the world outside was filled with peril. Sounds that once seemed mundane now sent him spiraling into panic. The clatter of chairs in the staff room would send his heart racing, reminiscent of the chaos that had ensued during the robbery. Each unexpected noise triggered a cascade of memories, making him feel as though he was reliving the event, amplifying the threat he felt from his surroundings. These memories not only deepened his fear but also made him question his own worth, leading him to believe that he had somehow failed to protect himself from harm. The world had become a cacophony of potential dangers, each sound a reminder of the injustice he felt — that someone had violated his sense of security and that nothing had been done to hold the perpetrators accountable. This belief only deepened his sense of helplessness, making it harder for him to shake off the memories that haunted him.

Ethan's internal narrative had shifted dramatically since the mugging. He frequently ruminated on how the institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. He could not shake the feeling that the police had been dismissive when he reported the incident, viewing him as just another victim in a city filled with crime. This sense of injustice only deepened with every flashback he experienced, further entrenching his belief that he was a target in an uncaring world, making him feel even more powerless. This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. Each time he recalled the robbery, he felt a surge of anger and betrayal that only served to reinforce his negative appraisals of his environment and the people within it.

In his classroom, Ethan tried to maintain a façade of normalcy, but his students could sense the change in him. He found himself avoiding driving with colleagues after school, as the thought of being in a confined space with others made him uneasy. The fear of being trapped felt all too real, a reflection of his ongoing battle with the trauma that loomed over him. This chronic sense of threat whispered to him that he was no longer in control, reinforcing his negative self-perception and convincing him that he was forever marked by the trauma he endured. He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful.

Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Ethan felt both a sense of relief and apprehension. He had finally sought help, driven by the overwhelming weight of his distress and the realization that he could no longer navigate this tumultuous sea of emotions alone. What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. Yet, deep down, he hoped to reclaim his life, to find a way to break free from the grip of his memories and allow himself to heal. Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Memory: The causal relationship between triggers and memory is absent; while triggers are mentioned, there is no explicit connection made that shows how triggers lead to the activation of memories.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The causal relationship between triggers and negative appraisals is absent; triggers are present, but no explanation connects them to the formation or reinforcement of negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The causal relationship between negative appraisals and memory is absent; while negative appraisals are detailed, there is no clear indication that they are derived from or influence specific memories.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Threat: The causal relationship between memory and threat is absent; although memories provoke feelings of threat, the connection implying that memories lead to a sense of threat is not explicitly stated.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The causal relationship between memory and negative appraisals is absent; memories are discussed in relation to feelings, but there is no clear link to how they contribute to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The causal relationship between threat and negative appraisals is absent; while a sense of threat is conveyed, the narrative does not clarify how this sense reinforces negative beliefs about the self or the world.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Threat → Triggers: The causal relationship between threat and triggers is absent; while both are mentioned, there is no direct indication that feelings of threat lead to the identification of new triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he felt that tightness in his chest, memories of the mugging rushed back with vivid clarity, making him relive the moment and reinforcing the belief that he was always in danger. 
<<<END>>>

<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every time he encountered those reminders, it solidified his belief that the world was an untrustworthy place, one where he was perpetually at risk. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The world had become a cacophony of potential dangers, each sound a reminder of the injustice he felt — that someone had violated his sense of security and that nothing had been done to hold the perpetrators accountable. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
These memories, steeped in the violence of that night, deepened his conviction that he was powerless, feeding into a belief that he was now marked by his trauma. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
These memories not only deepened his fear but also made him question his own worth, leading him to believe that he had somehow failed to protect himself from harm. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Every time a flashback surfaced, he was left grappling with the thought that he was not just a victim, but someone who had let this happen, which only reinforced his feelings of inadequacy. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
This perception of institutional failure compounded his sense of injustice, further entrenching him in the belief that the world was an inherently dangerous place. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
With the weight of that injustice pressing down on him, he felt an ever-present threat, as if the world was conspiring against him, confirming his fears that he was always unsafe. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
He had become increasingly isolated, withdrawing from social gatherings and even avoiding family outings, fearful that the memories would intrude and disrupt moments that should be joyful. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
The constant sense of threat that accompanied his isolation only reinforced his belief that he was a burden to those around him, further deepening his reluctance to engage with others. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
What frightened him most was the thought of remaining in this cycle of fear and avoidance, paralyzed by the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could never truly feel safe again. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
This ongoing threat loomed large in his mind, whispering to him that he was no longer the person he once was — someone who could trust the world and feel secure. 
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Recognizing how easily triggers could pull him back into the memories of that night made him feel even more disconnected from those he loved, further solidifying his belief that he was a burden. 
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time he felt that familiar surge of anxiety, he was reminded of the trauma that had altered his life so drastically, reinforcing the notion that he was not just a victim but someone forever changed by fear. 
<<<END>>>
